datos.marco.observado: This storm was measured on Mars: the Curiosity rover recorded the rise in radiation.
datos.marco.escenario: This real storm happened near Earth. In the game, we imagine it reaches your base.
datos.aviso: Unofficial project, not endorsed by NASA.
datos.tormenta.mock-tormenta-fuerte.queO: A big explosion on the Sun throws out a cloud of particles. It arrives in a day and a half.
datos.tormenta.mock-solo-fulguracion.que: The Sun flashes very bright for a moment, but the cloud is not coming our way.
datos.tormenta.mock-tormenta-marte.queOc: A slow cloud from the Sun reaches Mars and brings fast particles.
datos.marco.modelado: NASA's WSA-ENLIL model calculated that this cloud would reach Mars. It is a calculation, not a measurement.
datos.marco.rozando: According to the model, it would only graze it.
datos.tormenta.2024-05-14-x87.queOcurrio: The Sun let out one of its strongest flashes in years and a super-fast cloud of particles. It was not heading to Earth, but NASA's model calculated it would reach Mars.
datos.tormenta.2024-05-11-x58.queOcurrio: The same sunspot that painted auroras on Earth let out another strong flash and a fast cloud. Very energetic particles arrived near Earth, and NASA's model calculated the cloud would reach Mars.
datos.tormenta.2024-05-10-gannon.queOcur: Several clouds from the Sun hit Earth one after another. The magnetic storm reached the top of the scale and people saw auroras in many places.
datos.tormenta.2024-10-03-x90.queOcurrio: It was the strongest flash of this solar cycle up to that day. Its cloud caused a magnetic storm on Earth, and NASA's model calculated it would also reach Mars.
datos.tormenta.2024-10-10-g4.queOcurrio: A fast cloud from the Sun brought very energetic particles and a strong magnetic storm on Earth. NASA's model calculated it would also reach Mars.
datos.tormenta.2017-09-06-x93.queOcurrio: A sunspot let out a huge flash and a cloud that reached Earth and caused a magnetic storm.
datos.tormenta.2017-09-10-x82.queOcurrio: The same sunspot let out another huge flash and a super-fast cloud. Very energetic particles arrived near Earth.
datos.terreno.derivado: Ground height is a real measurement (MOLA and HRSC, via Mars Trek). Slope, light and shielding are game values the team calculated from that height; they are not measurements.
datos.terreno.sitio.llanura-central.desc: Flat ground and lots of sun, but out in the open: less protection.
datos.terreno.sitio.cerca-de-perseveranc: Close to where the Perseverance rover landed (Mars Trek marker). A bit of everything, nothing perfect.
At the foot of the south wall
The crater wall covers part of the sky: more protection, but the Sun hides earlier.
datos.terreno.sitio.sobre-el-borde-oeste: Up high you get tons of sun, but the ground is steep and there is less air above to protect you.
datos.tormenta.2024-05-20-marte.queOcurr: An explosion on the side of the Sun we can't see from Earth threw out a super-fast cloud. On Mars, the Curiosity rover measured that radiation went way up that same day.
datos.medicion.rad: Measured by the RAD instrument on the Curiosity rover, in Gale Crater on Mars (data from NASA OSDR RadLab). It is the dose the detector absorbs, in micrograys per hour.
datos.medicion.sinAumento: Curiosity did not measure a rise in radiation in those days.
datos.radiacion.comparacion: On the Moon, each day's radiation is almost double that on the Space Station. On Mars it is similar to the Station (but it was measured in different years, so the comparison is rough).
datos.ciencia.OSD-772.texto: On the Space Station, chile pepper plants grew for 137 days and made 26 peppers. Growing fresh food for astronauts is one of NASA's goals.
datos.ciencia.OSD-546.texto: Human cells that build bone spent about two weeks on the Space Station. There, they made about half as much calcium as the same cells on Earth.
datos.ciencia.OSD-360.texto: In a lab on Earth, scientists gave mice low doses of space-like radiation and saw changes in their bodies even months later. That is why shielding matters on trips to the Moon and Mars.
datos.glosario.sol.def: Our star. A giant ball of very hot gas that gives us light and heat.
datos.glosario.mancha-solar.def: A darker patch on the Sun where its magnetism gets tangled. Flares come from there.
datos.glosario.destello.def: A super bright flash of light on the Sun. The strongest ones are class X.
datos.glosario.nube-solar.def: A huge cloud of particles the Sun throws into space (scientists call it a CME). It can take days to arrive.
datos.glosario.particulas-energeticas.de: Tiny bits of atoms that travel super fast. They can harm bodies and machines.
datos.glosario.tormenta-magnetica.def: When a solar cloud shakes Earth's magnetism. It makes auroras.
datos.glosario.indice-kp.def: A number from 0 to 9 that says how strong a magnetic storm is on Earth.
datos.glosario.aurora.def: Colorful lights in the sky when particles from the Sun hit the air.
datos.glosario.radiacion.def: Invisible energy that travels through space. A lot of it is dangerous for astronauts.
datos.glosario.dosis.def: How much radiation something gets. Measured in sieverts (for people) or grays (what a detector absorbs).
datos.glosario.blindaje.def: A layer that blocks radiation, like thick walls, water or rock.
datos.glosario.crater.def: A round hole made by a space rock that crashed. Jezero is a crater on Mars.
datos.glosario.delta.def: A fan of dirt a river leaves when it reaches a lake. Jezero had one long ago.
datos.glosario.pendiente.def: How tilted the ground is. Landing on tilted ground is risky.
datos.glosario.modelo.def: A computer calculation that predicts what might happen. Sometimes it's right, sometimes not.
datos.glosario.curiosity.def: A NASA rover in Gale Crater on Mars. It has a radiation detector called RAD.
datos.glosario.perseverance.def: A NASA rover that landed in Jezero Crater on Mars.
datos.glosario.microgravedad.def: When you can barely feel your weight, like on the Space Station.
datos.usados.titulo: NASA data we used and why
datos.usados.donki: The storms are real: they come from DONKI, NASA's space weather database, with their code and date.
datos.usados.radlab: What happened on Mars was measured by the RAD detector on the Curiosity rover (data from NASA OSDR RadLab).
datos.usados.trek: The Jezero map comes from NASA Mars Trek: the ground height is real, and we used it to work out how flat, sunny and protected each place is.
datos.usados.osdr: The science cards tell about real experiments stored in NASA OSDR.
datos.usados.dosis: Radiation doses come from scientific papers: Mars from the Curiosity rover (NASA); the Moon and the Space Station from a study of China's Chang’e-4 mission.
datos.usados.noEnVivo: All this data is saved in the game: it is real, but not live.
datos.region.marte_polo_norte.descripcio: Near the north pole of Mars the Sun never climbs high: in midsummer it reaches about 33 degrees above the horizon at most, and in winter there are days when it doesn't rise at all. That's why getting solar energy is harder.
datos.region.derivado: The team calculated the Sun's height from the tilt of Mars's axis (25.19°, NASA). We don't have a terrain map for this region.
datos.artemis.titulo: Radiation on the Artemis I trip
datos.artemis.texto: In 2022 the Orion spacecraft of the Artemis I mission traveled around the Moon with no crew and radiation detectors inside. For most of the trip the radiation was about the same day after day, but shortly after launch it was about 480 times stronger for a while.
fuente.dosis.marte: RAD on the Curiosity rover (NASA), from Reitz et al. 2016
fuente.dosis.lunaIss: Zhang et al. 2020, China's Chang’e-4 mission (CNSA), not NASA
fuente.crater: Radiation near the Moon: CRaTER instrument on NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, via NASA OSDR RadLab. Real curated data, not live.
datos.luna.orbita: Measured by a spacecraft flying around the Moon, not on the ground.
datos.luna.medicion: Near the Moon, radiation went from {fondo} to {pico} µGy/h on {dia}: about {factor} times more than usual.
